one_liner: LD_PRELOAD heap profiler and leak finder for Linux; claims much lower overhead than Valgrind Massif or Memcheck, unmeasured.
what_it_does: A shared library (libmemtrail.so) plus a Python driver: `memtrail record ./app` preloads the library, which wraps malloc, calloc, realloc, posix_memalign, memalign, pvalloc, reallocarray and the C++ new/delete operators and streams every allocation event with its call stack to a gzip-compressed memtrail.data file. `memtrail report` then prints peak usage and leaks as call-stack trees with file:line (via addr2line) and writes JSON that gprof2dot turns into graphs. Programs can call memtrail_snapshot() from memtrail.h to mark extra snapshots; the call becomes a no-op when the library is not loaded.
how_it_is_fast: The program runs natively instead of under dynamic binary instrumentation: only allocator calls are intercepted, by symbol interposition through LD_PRELOAD, and they forward to __libc_malloc and __libc_free. Each call captures up to 32 return addresses with libunwind (statically linked and chosen because it does not call malloc), and the events are buffered in PIPE_BUF-sized chunks and piped to a forked `gzip --fast` child, so compression runs on another core. Symbol resolution and tree building are deferred to the offline Python report step.
when_to_use: Finding leaks or peak-memory call sites in long-running, CPU-heavy Linux programs that are too slow to finish under Valgrind Memcheck or Massif.
Unmodified binaries built with frame pointers or unwind tables, where you cannot recompile with AddressSanitizer or LeakSanitizer.
Mostly single-threaded or lightly threaded code with moderate allocation rates, since every event takes one global lock.
Taking peak and leak snapshots at chosen points in a run by calling memtrail_snapshot() from the program.
when_not_to_use: Highly multi-threaded, allocation-heavy servers: every malloc and free takes one process-wide recursive pthread mutex, so allocations are serialized across threads.

Programs with many small allocations and tight memory: each block carries a header with a 32-entry return-address array plus list links, size and pointer (over 280 bytes on x86-64), and the library stops the program with _exit(1) once tracked bytes pass half of physical RAM.
Bug hunting for use-after-free, overflows or uninitialized reads: it only accounts allocations; use Memcheck, AddressSanitizer or Dr. Memory.
Non-Linux platforms: it relies on LD_PRELOAD, glibc's __libc_malloc and PTHREAD_RECURSIVE_MUTEX_INITIALIZER_NP; the header is a no-op elsewhere.
Cases where you need a measured overhead figure: the README gives none, and benchmark.cpp with `make bench` only times the report step.

integration.form: shared lib (LD_PRELOAD) plus Python 3 driver script
integration.dependencies: libunwind (bundled git submodule, built static), Python 3, gzip, binutils addr2line; gprof2dot for graphs
integration.min_toolchain: C++17 (gnu++17), g++ by default, autotools to build the bundled libunwind
integration.platforms: Linux with glibc; x86-64 assumed for 16-byte minimum alignment, other architectures fall back to sizeof(double) alignment
integration.thread_safety: thread-safe through one global recursive mutex around all bookkeeping
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — like Valgrind it runs unmodified binaries, but it replaces only Massif- and leak-check-style accounting, not Memcheck's error detection

gotchas: Allocations made before the library has opened its output file (for example libstdc++'s emergency pool) are marked internal and left out of totals.
Freed blocks that were already logged stay on a pending list until the next flush, so the process's real RSS under memtrail can stay above its native peak.
Allocator calls re-entered while the lock is held are marked internal and print 'memtrail: warning: recursion', so they are missing from the report.

Licensing: there is no LICENSE file and GitHub shows none, but memtrail.cpp, memtrail.h and the memtrail script carry MIT permission headers (Copyright 2011-2019 Jose Fonseca), so the code can be reused under those terms.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Choose it over heaptrack or bytehound when you want a small, self-contained tool with a pipe-to-gzip recorder and gprof2dot output; prefer heaptrack for multi-threaded programs (it does not serialize threads, per its README) and tracing_malloc when you want a published runtime number against Valgrind.
verified_claims_summary: No measurement exists: the README says only 'very little runtime overhead' and that the author's workloads ran too slowly under Valgrind's dynamic binary instrumentation. The repo's benchmark.cpp drives 262,144 4-byte allocations through random 8-deep call chains, but the `make bench` target times only `memtrail report`, not the profiled run against native or Valgrind.
status_note: Active (commits on 2026-04-26 add tests and coverage, 188 commits, 0 open issues, 89 stars); MIT terms sit in the file headers despite the missing LICENSE file, so it is usable, but the speed claim against Valgrind is unmeasured.
